**Michael Bayer ([@zzzeek](https://github.com/zzzeek)) wrote:**

for oracle, we disallow FOR UPDATE on the inner select, if we allow:


```
diff --git a/lib/sqlalchemy/dialects/oracle/base.py b/lib/sqlalchemy/dialects/oracle/base.py
index e55a9cbc6..2cbc5b544 100644
--- a/lib/sqlalchemy/dialects/oracle/base.py
+++ b/lib/sqlalchemy/dialects/oracle/base.py
@@ -921,8 +921,8 @@ class OracleCompiler(compiler.SQLCompiler):
         return ""
 
     def for_update_clause(self, select, **kw):
-        if self.is_subquery():
-            return ""
+        #if self.is_subquery():
+        #    return ""
 
         tmp = ' FOR UPDATE'
 

```

then we get:

```
 ORA-00907: missing right parenthesis [SQL: 'SELECT anon_1.a_id AS anon_1_a_id, b_1.id AS b_1_id, b_1.a_id AS b_1_a_id \nFROM (SELECT a_id \nFROM (SELECT a.id AS a_id \nFROM a FOR UPDATE) \nWHERE ROWNUM <= :param_1 FOR UPDATE) anon_1 LEFT OUTER JOIN b b_1 ON anon_1.a_id = b_1.a_id'] [parameters: {'param_1': 1}] 
```

so the behavior of "FOR UPDATE" applying to inner queries, or not, needs to be figured out totally, and a platform-agnostic solution must be devised, such that a FOR UPDATE goes in the "correct" place in a backend agnostic way.

**Michael Bayer ([@zzzeek](https://github.com/zzzeek)) wrote:**

[postgresql](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/9.0/static/sql-select.html#SQL-FOR-UPDATE-SHARE):  

> FOR UPDATE causes the rows retrieved by the SELECT statement to be locked as though for update. This prevents them from being modified or deleted by other transactions until the current transaction ends. That is, other transactions that attempt UPDATE, DELETE, or SELECT FOR UPDATE of these rows will be blocked until the current transaction ends. Also, if an UPDATE, DELETE, or SELECT FOR UPDATE from another transaction has already locked a selected row or rows, SELECT FOR UPDATE will wait for the other transaction to complete, and will then lock and return the updated row (or no row, if the row was deleted). Within a SERIALIZABLE transaction, however, an error will be thrown if a row to be locked has changed since the transaction started. For further discussion see Chapter 13.

e.g. lock all tables

[oracle](http://www.dba-oracle.com/t_adv_plsql_for_update_where_current.htm): 

> When we want to issue a lock over the record set returned by the cursor associated SELECT query, we can opt for the FOR UPDATE clause, which automatically places an exclusive row-level lock on all the rows retrieved, forbidding any other session from performing a DML operation on them until we perform a commit or a rollback to release the lock.

e.g. lock all tables

[mysql](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.0/en/innodb-locking-reads.html):

> If a row is locked by a transaction, a SELECT ... FOR UPDATE or SELECT ... FOR SHARE transaction that requests the same locked row must wait until the blocking transaction releases the row lock. This behavior prevents transactions from updating or deleting rows that are queried for updates by other transactions. However, waiting for a row lock to be released is not necessary if you want the query to return immediately when a requested row is locked, or if excluding locked rows from the result set is acceptable. 

this says nothing about only locking rows within tables that are not inside of subqueries.

@juliennakache can you please further support your assertion that "In my case, it seems that the with_for_update only locked the joinedtable because the FOR UPDATE statement is only applied to the joinedtable - the root table is not locked because it is queried via the subselect. " ?     this would be a *huge* issue to deal with if this is the case and we need 100% positive information that this is the case, thanks.

**Jay Pipes ([@jaypipes](https://github.com/jaypipes)) wrote:**

Hi Julien,

I noticed that the SQL being generated for your application is actually non-deterministic:

```sql
SELECT anon_1.telemedicine_consultation_id AS anon_1_telemedicine_consultation_id, anon_1.telemedicine_consultation_consultation_uuid AS anon_1_telemedicine_consultation_consultation_uuid, anon_1.telemedicine_consultation_patient_member_id AS anon_1_telemedicine_consultation_patient_member_id, consultation_action_1_id, consultation_action_1.consultation_uuid AS consultation_action_1_consultation_uuid, consultation_action_1.action_type AS consultation_action_1_action_type
FROM (

    SELECT telemedicine.consultation.id AS telemedicine_consultation_id, telemedicine.consultation.consultation_uuid AS telemedicine_consultation_consultation_uuid, telemedicine.consultation.patient_member_id AS telemedicine_consultation_patient_member_id
    FROM telemedicine.consultation 
    WHERE telemedicine.consultation.consultation_uuid = %s
    LIMIT %s

 ) AS anon_1 LEFT OUTER JOIN telemedicine.consultation_action AS consultation_action_1 ON anon_1.telemedicine_consultation_consultation_uuid = consultation_action_1.consultation_uuid ORDER BY consultation_action_1.id DESC FOR UPDATE;
```

You will note that the derived table (the subquery in the FROM clause) has a LIMIT expression on it, but no ORDER BY clause. This makes the inner selection in that derived table non-deterministic and therefore I'm pretty sure that the FOR UPDATE clause is not able to be applied to the JOIN condition because there is no determinism in looking up the read view for other transactions that might be interested in the data from the end selection.

Try adding an ORDER BY clause on the derived table and seeing if the behaviour changes.

Best,
-jay

**Jay Pipes ([@jaypipes](https://github.com/jaypipes)) wrote:**

Thanks, Julien. After some digging around today with Mike, it looks like this is a bug in MySQL's handling of subqueries. Converting the query to use standard JOINs does fix the issue. The only reason for the use of the subquery is (AFAICT) to allow a LIMIT to be expressed on the inner query that doesn't affect the outer query. However, as you say, the UUID field is unique and therefore there shouldn't be a need to have a LIMIT clause on the inner query at all. So, long story short, we need to figure out why, if the UUID field is indeed unique, why this subquery is generated to begin with...

**Michael Bayer ([@zzzeek](https://github.com/zzzeek)) wrote:**

Render FOR UPDATE on the inner subquery as well as the outer

The ORM now doubles the "FOR UPDATE" clause within the subquery that
renders in conjunction with joined eager loading in some cases, as it has
been observed that MySQL does not lock the rows from a subquery.   This
means the query renders with two FOR UPDATE clauses; note that on some
backends such as Oracle, FOR UPDATE clauses on subqueries are silently
ignored since they are unnecessary.  Additionally, in the case of the "OF"
clause used primarily with Postgresql, the FOR UPDATE is rendered only on
the inner subquery when this is used so that the selectable can be targeted
to the table within the SELECT statement.
